d.d: Synonym of Vote (“person from Votia or of Votic descent”).
A formalized choice on legally relevant measures such as employment or appointment to office or a proceeding about a legal dispute.
d.x: The city council decided the matter should go to public vote.

d.d: An act or instance of participating in such a choice, e.g., by submitting a ballot.
d.x: The Supreme Court upheld the principle of one person, one vote.

d.d: Any judgment of intellect leading not only to a formal opinion but also to a particular choice in a legally relevant measure, a point of view as published.
d.x: dissenting vote (i.e. in particular the differing opinion published with a judicial judgment considered as a source of information)

d.d: To cast a vote; to assert a formalized choice in an election.
d.x: Q: Did you vote last month? A: Yes. I voted for John Smith, and it's a shame that he lost; you can't blame me for the mess we're in now.

d.d: To choose or grant (some objective) by means of a vote, or by general consent.
d.x: The directors voted an increase in R&D spending.

d.d: To exercise one's voting right upon (a ballot or a share of stock).
That has been assigned or established by a vote.

Dedicated or given in fulfillment of a vow or pledge.
d.x: She placed a votive offering at the shrine.

d.d: Of, expressing, or symbolizing a vow. Often used to describe thick cylindrical candles found in many churches, lit when making a private vow or asking a private intention.
d.x: The church was lit by votive candles.
